vignette:
David was 54 when the assault happened, three years before he finally sat in a therapist's office. He had been working as a private tutor for over a decade, mostly meeting high school and college students in libraries or their homes. One of his regulars was a man in his twenties, someone David had tutored for months without incident. Then one evening, after a session that ran late, the man cornered him in the study, pressed him against the wall, and forced his hands onto David's body while demanding that David return the touch. David froze-his body would not move, would not shout. Later, he could describe only fragments: the weight of the man's chest, the carpet against his cheek, the sound of his own breathing. The rest was a cavern of missing seconds. For weeks he could not find words to explain what had happened, even to himself. He told no one.

In the months that followed, David began to notice that physical touch-a student's accidental brush on the arm, a handshake from a colleague-sent a jolt through him that felt like the start of the assault. The trigger would yank the memory back whole, vivid and sharp, and at the same time it would flood him with the conviction that his body could not be trusted, that it had failed him once and might fail again. That feeling of body unreliability made him even more watchful: he started scanning rooms for anyone who might stand too close, especially men. And that same belief-that his body had betrayed him-kept pulling him back into the memory, replaying the moment of his paralysis as though he needed to understand how his own flesh had turned against him. He became certain that he had to be constantly careful because danger could erupt from anywhere. The relentless sense of threat quietly confirmed what he had been dreading: that he was no longer the person he had been before, that the assault had changed something irreparable inside him. When he was in that hypervigilant state, the memory of the assault would often surface with it, as if his own heightened alert had opened a door to the past. The more he believed that, the more he avoided unfamiliar places-new coffee shops, the library annex-where he could not assess the exits or the people. At the same time, the memory itself, when it surfaced unbidden, would reignite the same threat monitoring, making him tighten his shoulders and search for the nearest door. He began always choosing a seat with his back to the wall, preferably near an exit, and he watched other people for signs of threat so closely that his eyes ached by the end of a tutoring session.

His negative appraisals-the isolation he felt, the sense that he was set apart from others because no one could understand-also drove his maladaptive strategies. Believing that his body was unreliable and that he had to be on constant guard made him avoid any situation likely to stir strong emotions, because he was afraid of losing control. The conviction that he was fundamentally different from others also meant that ordinary physical contact-a handshake, a pat on the back-now felt dangerous and likely to trigger him, so that even the slightest touch became a potential threat. He also avoided all forms of physical contact, turning down hugs from friends, stepping away when someone reached toward him. And he started smoking more-half a pack a day, then a full pack-because the ritual of lighting up gave him something to do with his hands when anxiety spiked, and the numbness felt like a small shield. The link worked the other way too: whenever a memory of the assault intruded-vivid, detail-laden, yet still fragmented-it strengthened his belief that he was fundamentally separate from other people, that his body had marked him as different. That same memory could also act as a trigger itself, making him feel a ghost of the forced touch, which then escalated his vigilance and sent him reaching for a cigarette.

Now, at fifty-seven, David's world has narrowed almost entirely. He still tutors, but only female students, and he meets them in public libraries where he can scan the room before choosing a seat. Last month a male student accidentally brushed his shoulder, and David flinched so violently that the student asked if he was okay. David said nothing, but the moment replayed for days. What finally brought him to seek help was not the flinch itself but the loneliness: he realized he had not let anyone hug him in three years, and that the constant wariness was exhausting him. He is most afraid that talking about it will make the memories sharper, but underneath that he is equally afraid that he will never feel safe again-that his own vigilance has become the thing he cannot escape.

vignette_attempts.feedback:
REQUIRED EDGES MISSING:
- Negative Appraisals → Memory: No paragraph conveys that the patient's negative appraisals (e.g., body unreliability) cause or lead to intrusive memories of the assault.
  e.g. "The belief that she was permanently changed kept bringing her back to the moment it had happened, as if she needed to locate exactly where she had been lost."
  e.g. "Telling herself that she should have seen it coming made the memory more vivid and easier to find — it sat there waiting, proof of her failure."
  e.g. "The conviction that she was weak fed directly into the flashback, colouring it, making it worse: she wasn't just there again, she was there again and helpless."
- Negative Appraisals → Triggers: No paragraph conveys that the patient's negative appraisals (e.g., being set apart) cause or increase triggers (e.g., physical touch).
  e.g. "Once she had concluded that the world was fundamentally unsafe, almost anything could confirm it — a figure in her periphery, the wrong tone of voice, footsteps behind her."
  e.g. "The belief that she couldn't trust her own judgement meant that things she would once have registered and dismissed now snagged and held her attention."
  e.g. "Her conviction that it would happen again meant she moved through ordinary days as if they were mined — every ambiguity became a potential signal."
- Threat → Memory: No paragraph conveys that the patient's sense of threat (e.g., feeling of danger) causes or leads to intrusive memories of the assault.
  e.g. "Walking home on high alert, she passed a doorway and the memory was simply there — pulled out of her by the adrenaline, fully formed."
  e.g. "The persistent sense of danger kept her close to the event in her mind, as if she needed to keep reviewing it to stay one step ahead of whatever came next."
  e.g. "On nights when the threat felt highest, the memory was hardest to keep at bay — it would surface in the dark, vivid and unwelcome."
